claim: Planar supported lipid bilayers (PSLB) presenting T cell receptor (TCR) ligands and ICAM-1 induce budding of extracellular microvesicles enriched in functional TCR from helper T cells.
source: Planar supported lipid bilayers (PSLB) presenting T cell receptor (TCR) ligands and ICAM-1 induce budding of extracellular microvesicles enriched in functional TCR, defined here as synaptic ectosomes (SE), from helper T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Synaptic ectosomes (SE) are defined as TCR enriched extracellular vesicles that bud directly into the synaptic cleft from the T cell side of the immunological synapse.
source: Planar supported lipid bilayers (PSLB) presenting T cell receptor (TCR) ligands and ICAM-1 induce budding of extracellular microvesicles enriched in functional TCR, defined here as synaptic ectosomes (SE), from helper T cells.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines SE in the abstract.

claim: SE bind peptide-MHC directly exporting TCR into the synaptic cleft.
source: SE bind peptide-MHC directly exporting TCR into the synaptic cleft, but incorporation of other effectors is unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as prior knowledge.

claim: CD40L is selectively enriched in SE in response to addition of CD40 to SLB presenting TCR ligands and ICAM-1.
source: We demonstrate selective enrichment of CD40L and ICOS in SE in response to addition of CD40 and ICOSL, respectively, to SLB presenting TCR ligands and ICAM-1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: ICOS is selectively enriched in SE in response to addition of ICOSL to SLB presenting TCR ligands and ICAM-1.
source: We demonstrate selective enrichment of CD40L and ICOS in SE in response to addition of CD40 and ICOSL, respectively, to SLB presenting TCR ligands and ICAM-1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: SE are enriched in tetraspanins.
source: SE are enriched in tetraspanins, BST-2, TCR signaling and ESCRT proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry and mass spectrometry data.

claim: SE are enriched in BST-2.
source: SE are enriched in tetraspanins, BST-2, TCR signaling and ESCRT proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry and mass spectrometry data.

claim: SE are enriched in TCR signaling proteins.
source: SE are enriched in tetraspanins, BST-2, TCR signaling and ESCRT proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: SE are enriched in ESCRT proteins.
source: SE are enriched in tetraspanins, BST-2, TCR signaling and ESCRT proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: CD40L is present in microclusters within CD81 defined SE that are spatially segregated from TCR/ICOS/BST-2.
source: Super-resolution microscopy demonstrated that CD40L is present in microclusters within CD81 defined SE that are spatially segregated from TCR/ICOS/BST-2.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by dSTORM imaging data.

claim: CD40L+ SE retain the capacity to induce dendritic cell maturation.
source: CD40L+ SE retain the capacity to induce dendritic cell maturation and cytokine production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by dendritic cell activation experiments.

claim: CD40L+ SE retain the capacity to induce cytokine production in dendritic cells.
source: CD40L+ SE retain the capacity to induce dendritic cell maturation and cytokine production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cytokine array data.

claim: The immunological synapse (IS) is a platform for signal integration.
source: However, the IS is not only a platform for signal integration, but also enables polarized delivery of effector function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The immunological synapse enables polarized delivery of effector function.
source: However, the IS is not only a platform for signal integration, but also enables polarized delivery of effector function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The IS enables polarized delivery of cytokines.
source: These include the polarized delivery of cytokines (Huse et al., 2006), nucleic acid containing exosomes (Mittelbrunn et al., 2011), and TCR enriched extracellular vesicles that bud directly into the synaptic cleft from the T cell side of the IS (Choudhuri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: The IS enables polarized delivery of nucleic acid containing exosomes.
source: These include the polarized delivery of cytokines (Huse et al., 2006), nucleic acid containing exosomes (Mittelbrunn et al., 2011), and TCR enriched extracellular vesicles that bud directly into the synaptic cleft from the T cell side of the IS (Choudhuri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: The IS enables polarized delivery of TCR enriched extracellular vesicles that bud directly into the synaptic cleft from the T cell side.
source: These include the polarized delivery of cytokines (Huse et al., 2006), nucleic acid containing exosomes (Mittelbrunn et al., 2011), and TCR enriched extracellular vesicles that bud directly into the synaptic cleft from the T cell side of the IS (Choudhuri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: CD40 ligand (CD40L, CD154) is a 39 kDa glycoprotein expressed by CD4+ T cells.
source: CD40 ligand (CD40L, CD154) is a 39 kDa glycoprotein expressed by CD4+ T cells (Noelle et al., 1992) and is one of the key effectors delivered by helper T cells through the IS (Ridge et al., 1998; Schoenberger et al., 1998).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: CD40L is one of the key effectors delivered by helper T cells through the IS.
source: CD40 ligand (CD40L, CD154) is a 39 kDa glycoprotein expressed by CD4+ T cells (Noelle et al., 1992) and is one of the key effectors delivered by helper T cells through the IS (Ridge et al., 1998; Schoenberger et al., 1998).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: ICOS interaction with ICOSL promotes CD40L-CD40 interactions in the IS.
source: Inducible T cell costimulator (ICOS, also known at CD278) interaction with ICOSL promotes CD40L-CD40 interactions in the IS (Liu et al., 2015; Papa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: CD40L is transferred to antigen presenting cells in vitro.
source: CD40L is transferred to antigen presenting cells in vitro (Gardell and Parker, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: Trimeric CD40L released by proteolysis by ADAM10 is a partial agonist of CD40.
source: Trimeric CD40L released by proteolysis by ADAM10 is a partial agonist of CD40, suggesting the fully active CD40 must remain membrane anchored to sufficiently crosslink CD40 for full agonist function (Yacoub et al., 2013; Haswell et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: Fully active CD40L must remain membrane anchored to sufficiently crosslink CD40 for full agonist function.
source: Trimeric CD40L released by proteolysis by ADAM10 is a partial agonist of CD40, suggesting the fully active CD40 must remain membrane anchored to sufficiently crosslink CD40 for full agonist function (Yacoub et al., 2013; Haswell et al., 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from cited literature.

claim: Minimal IS CD40L was detected in the absence of CD40.
source: Minimal IS CD40L was detected in the absence of CD40 as previously reported (Papa et al., 2017) and near uniformly increased anti-CD40L was detected at 10, 50 and 100 CD40 molec./µm2 with a reduction in signal at 500 CD40 molec./µm2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by TIRFM data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Near uniformly increased anti-CD40L was detected at 10, 50 and 100 CD40 molec./µm2.
source: Minimal IS CD40L was detected in the absence of CD40 as previously reported (Papa et al., 2017) and near uniformly increased anti-CD40L was detected at 10, 50 and 100 CD40 molec./µm2 with a reduction in signal at 500 CD40 molec./µm2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by TIRFM data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A reduction in anti-CD40L signal was observed at 500 CD40 molec./µm2.
source: Minimal IS CD40L was detected in the absence of CD40 as previously reported (Papa et al., 2017) and near uniformly increased anti-CD40L was detected at 10, 50 and 100 CD40 molec./µm2 with a reduction in signal at 500 CD40 molec./µm2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by TIRFM data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CD40L can be detected and localized over the entire physiological range of CD40 densities using anti-CD40L antibody.
source: Thus, whether this loss of signal at high CD40 density is due to competition between CD40 and the anti-CD40L mAb or some other process, we conclude that CD40L can be detected and localized over the entire physiological range of CD40 densities using anti-CD40L antibody.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1B.

claim: On PSLB with ICAM-1 only, most of the CD40L signal was intracellular with rare evidence of CD40L puncta at or near the cell surface.
source: On PSLB with ICAM-1 only, most of the CD40L signal was intracellular with rare evidence of CD40L puncta at or near the cell surface based on comparison to the CellMask signal and adding CD40 in the bilayer did not alter this profile (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by Airyscan confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Adding CD40 to PSLB with ICAM-1 only did not alter the intracellular CD40L profile.
source: On PSLB with ICAM-1 only, most of the CD40L signal was intracellular with rare evidence of CD40L puncta at or near the cell surface based on comparison to the CellMask signal and adding CD40 in the bilayer did not alter this profile (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by Airyscan confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: On PSLB presenting ICAM1 and UCHT1-Fab, but without CD40, the cell interior was mostly depleted of CD40L and CD40L puncta were distributed over or near the cell surface.
source: On PSLB presenting ICAM1 and UCHT1-Fab, but without CD40, the cell interior was mostly depleted of CD40L and CD40L puncta were distributed over or near the cell surface, often appearing at the ends of small projections (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Airyscan confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: On PSLB with ICAM-1, UCHT1-Fab and CD40, most of the CD40L was concentrated in the center of the IS and appeared to be just outside the CellMask signal.
source: On PSLB with ICAM-1, UCHT1-Fab and CD40, most of the CD40L was concentrated in the center of the IS and appeared to be just outside the CellMask signal (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Airyscan confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CD40L was detected in puncta in the IS just after and together with TCR-UCHT1-Fab complexes.
source: Live microscopy demonstrated that CD40L was detected in puncta in the IS just after and together with TCR-UCHT1-Fab complexes (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by live microscopy data shown in Video 1.

claim: When T cells break IS symmetry and transition to migratory kinapses they leave trails of SE behind on the substrate.
source: When T cells break IS symmetry and transition to migratory kinapses they leave trails of SE behind on the substrate (Choudhuri et al., 2014) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: In the absence of CD40 in the PSLB, the few anti-CD40L reactive puncta that were detected remained associated with the migrating T cell.
source: In the absence of CD40 in the PSLB, the few anti-CD40L reactive puncta that were detected remained associated with the migrating T cell (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by TIRFM data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Kinapses formed in the presence of CD40 resulted in a trail of anti-CD40L reactive puncta that remained tethered to the PSLB.
source: Kinapses formed in the presence of CD40 resulted in a trail of anti-CD40L reactive puncta that remained tethered to the PSLB (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by TIRFM data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: BSLB have been used previously to demonstrate activity of purified MHC proteins.
source: BSLB have been used previously to demonstrate activity of purified MHC proteins (Gay et al., 1986), detect weak protein interactions (Baksh et al., 2004) and determine biophysical requirements for phagocytosis (Bakalar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: BSLB have been used to detect weak protein interactions.
source: BSLB have been used previously to demonstrate activity of purified MHC proteins (Gay et al., 1986), detect weak protein interactions (Baksh et al., 2004) and determine biophysical requirements for phagocytosis (Bakalar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: BSLB have been used to determine biophysical requirements for phagocytosis.
source: BSLB have been used previously to demonstrate activity of purified MHC proteins (Gay et al., 1986), detect weak protein interactions (Baksh et al., 2004) and determine biophysical requirements for phagocytosis (Bakalar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: Transfer of TCR was ligand dose dependent and independent of ICOSL and CD40.
source: Transfer of TCR was ligand dose dependent and independent of ICOSL and CD40.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2F.

claim: ICOS was weakly transferred in response to ICOSL without UCHT1-Fab in the BSLB.
source: ICOS was weakly transferred in response to ICOSL without UCHT1-Fab in the BSLB, but the efficiency was increased by TCR engagement.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2F.

claim: The efficiency of ICOS transfer was increased by TCR engagement.
source: ICOS was weakly transferred in response to ICOSL without UCHT1-Fab in the BSLB, but the efficiency was increased by TCR engagement.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2F.

claim: CD40L was transferred only when UCHT1-Fab and CD40 was present in the BSLB.
source: CD40L was transferred only when UCHT1-Fab and CD40 was present in the BSLB, and we were not able to detect a substantial increase when ICOSL was also included in the BSLB in contrast to prior results with PSLB (Papa et al., 2017) (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2F and supplements.

claim: ICOSL presentation on BSLB increased conjugate formation between T cells and BSLB.
source: However, ICOSL presentation on BSLB increased conjugate formation between T cells and BSLB and also enhanced transfer of ICOS and tetraspanins (more significantly CD63) from T cell to BSLB in a manner depending upon the density of ICOSL and the dose of UCHT1-Fab (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2 supplements.

claim: ICOSL presentation on BSLB enhanced transfer of ICOS from T cell to BSLB in a manner depending upon the density of ICOSL and the dose of UCHT1-Fab.
source: However, ICOSL presentation on BSLB increased conjugate formation between T cells and BSLB and also enhanced transfer of ICOS and tetraspanins (more significantly CD63) from T cell to BSLB in a manner depending upon the density of ICOSL and the dose of UCHT1-Fab (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2 supplements.

claim: ICOSL presentation on BSLB enhanced transfer of tetraspanins (more significantly CD63) from T cell to BSLB in a manner depending upon the density of ICOSL and the dose of UCHT1-Fab.
source: However, ICOSL presentation on BSLB increased conjugate formation between T cells and BSLB and also enhanced transfer of ICOS and tetraspanins (more significantly CD63) from T cell to BSLB in a manner depending upon the density of ICOSL and the dose of UCHT1-Fab (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2 supplements.

claim: The most enriched (>10% transfer) class of non-ligated proteins are BST-2 (Tetherin) and the tetraspanins CD9, CD63, CD81 and CD82.
source: The most enriched (>10% transfer) class of non-ligated proteins are BST-2 (Tetherin) and the tetraspanins CD9, CD63, CD81 and CD82 (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2D and supplements.

claim: HLA-ABC was enriched in SE at an intermediate level (1–10%).
source: HLA-ABC was enriched in SE at an intermediate level (1–10%) along with other proteins including CD2, CD6 and CD49D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2F.

claim: LFA-1, CD38 and LAMP-1 (CD107a) were represented at < 1% and were not enriched above the ordinary levels found in the plasma membrane.
source: LFA-1, CD38 and LAMP-1 (CD107a)were represented at < 1% and were not enriched above the ordinary levels found in the plasma membrane (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2F.

claim: LFA-1 is ligated by ICAM-1 on the BSLB and was not enriched in the SE from the CD4+ effector T cells.
source: Its notable that LFA-1 is ligated by ICAM-1 on the BSLB and was not enriched in the SE from the CD4+ effector T cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2F.

claim: CD40L localizes to the center of the IS predominantly in the presence of CD40 and HLA-DRB1*09:01-influenza HA338-355, not in the presence of HLA-DRB1*09:01:CLIP.
source: On PSLB, CD40L localizes to the center of the IS predominantly in the presence of CD40 and HLA-DRB1*09:01-influenza HA338-355, not in the presence of HLA-DRB1*09:01:CLIP (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TIRFM data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: BST2 was co-localized in the TCR in an antigen dependent manner.
source: BST2 was also co-localized in the TCR in an antigen dependent manner (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TIRFM data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Some ICOS transferred to BSLB with ICOSL with control HLA-DRB1*09:01:CLIP or in the absence of any MHC molecules.
source: As with the polyclonal CD4+ T cells, some ICOS transferred to BSLB with ICOSL with control HLA-DRB1*09:01:CLIP or in the absence of any MHC molecules (Figure 2G), a phenomenon which is accompanied by the recruitment of ICOSL to a TCR independent cSMAC-like structure on the PSLB (Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry and TIRFM data in Figures 2G and 3C,E.

claim: ICOSL is recruited to a TCR independent cSMAC-like structure on the PSLB.
source: As with the polyclonal CD4+ T cells, some ICOS transferred to BSLB with ICOSL with control HLA-DRB1*09:01:CLIP or in the absence of any MHC molecules (Figure 2G), a phenomenon which is accompanied by the recruitment of ICOSL to a TCR independent cSMAC-like structure on the PSLB (Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TIRFM data in Figure 3C,E.

claim: The ICOSL driven TCR independent synapse may exert some control over migration of T cells, but it did not lead to CD40L transfer.
source: This ICOSL driven TCR independent synapse may exert some control over migration of T cells, but it did not lead to CD40L transfer.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is an inference from the data.

claim: TCR engagement is not absolutely necessary for CD40L transfer.
source: PMA-ionomycin significantly increased the relative transfer of CD40L to BSLB with 0 or 20 molec./µm2 UCHT1-Fab (Figure 4B). This demonstrates that TCR engagement is not absolutely necessary for CD40L transfer.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4B.

claim: STRING analysis of 130 candidates having an absolute fold change (+UCHT1-Fab /- UCHT1 Fab) of at least 3.35 revealed a network of proteins with reported interactions.
source: STRING analysis of 130 candidates having an absolute fold change (+UCHT1-Fab /- UCHT1 Fab) of at least 3.35 revealed a network of proteins with reported interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 5A.

claim: Reactome analysis revealed significant enrichment of TCR signaling, vesicle mediated transport and ESCRT machinery pathways.
source: This analysis revealed significant enrichment of TCR signaling, vesicle mediated transport and ESCRT machinery pathways (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Reactome analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: Several surface proteins identified as enriched in the immunofluorescence analysis were also enriched in SE as defined by MS including CD40L, ICOS, CD81, CD82, BST2, HLA-A, HLA-B, CD2, CD6 and CD49d (ITGA4/ITGB1).
source: Several surface proteins identified as enriched in the immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 2D) were also enriched in SE as defined by MS including CD40L, ICOS, CD81, CD82, BST2, HLA-A, HLA-B, CD2, CD6 and CD49d (ITGA4/ITGB1) (Figure 5A, and supplement excel file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 5A.

claim: Most of the surface proteins that were not enriched in the immunofluorescence analysis were also not detected in the MS analysis including CD4, CD27, CD38, CD45, CD80, OX40, GITR and LAMP1.
source: Most of the surface proteins that were not enriched in the immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 2D) were also not detected in the MS analysis including CD4, CD27, CD38, CD45, CD80, OX40, GITR and LAMP1 (Figure 5A, and supplement excel file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 5A.

claim: ESCRT-0 components HRS, STAM2 and EPN1, ESCRT-II component ALIX ESCRT-III component CHMP4b were enhanced on BSLB by TCR engagement.
source: ESCRT-0 components HRS, STAM2 and EPN1, ESCRT-II component ALIX ESCRT-III component CHMP4b were enhanced on BSLB by TCR engagement (Figure 5A, and supplement excel file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 5A.

claim: EPN1 and ALIX were localized in or around the cSMAC.
source: Within the range of TIRF microscopy, EPN1 and ALIX were localized in or around the cSMAC (Figure 5D,E), whereas STAM2 was present in the cSMAC, but also in peripheral components of the IS, consistent with additional functions of STAM2 in the IS (Bache et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TIRFM data in Figure 5D,E.

claim: STAM2 was present in the cSMAC, but also in peripheral components of the IS.
source: Within the range of TIRF microscopy, EPN1 and ALIX were localized in or around the cSMAC (Figure 5D,E), whereas STAM2 was present in the cSMAC, but also in peripheral components of the IS, consistent with additional functions of STAM2 in the IS (Bache et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TIRFM data in Figure 5D,E.

claim: EPN1 was co-localized with UCHT1-Fab in the cSMAC formed on PSLB also presenting ICAM-1 together with CD40.
source: Airyscan confocal microscopy revealed that EPN1 was co-localized with UCHT1-Fab in the cSMAC formed on PSLB also presenting ICAM-1 together with CD40 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Airyscan confocal microscopy data in Figure 5 supplement 1.

claim: Both EPN1 and CHMP4b suppression resulted in a significant reduction of CD40L transfer to BSLB, which was not observed for TCR.
source: Both EPN1 and CHMP4b suppression resulted in a significant reduction of CD40L transfer to BSLB, which was not observed for TCR (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by CRISPR gene editing and flow cytometry data in Figure 5F and supplement 2.

claim: A similar trend was observed for Alix, which slightly reduced CD40L but not TCR transfer, suggesting a differential role of EPN1, CHMP4b and ALIX in the regulation of sorting and release of CD40L on SE.
source: Interestingly, a similar trend was observed for Alix, which slightly reduced CD40L but not TCR transfer, suggesting a differential role of EPN1, CHMP4b and ALIX in the regulation of sorting and release of CD40L on SE (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by CRISPR gene editing and flow cytometry data in Figure 5F and supplement 2.

claim: The synaptic transfer of CD81 was reduced by suppression of ALIX, EPN1, CHMP4b, TSG101 and VPS4b proteins.
source: As expected, the synaptic transfer of CD81 was also reduced by suppression of ALIX, EPN1, CHMP4b, TSG101 and VPS4b proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by CRISPR gene editing and flow cytometry data in Figure 5 supplement 2.

claim: Suppression of ALIX had no effect on transfer of TCR and CD40L, suggesting a potential degree of redundancy of ESCRT involved in the release of SE at the IS.
source: On the other hand, suppression of ALIX had no effect on transfer of TCR and CD40L, suggesting a potential degree of redundancy of ESCRT involved in the release of SE at the IS.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is an inference from the data.

claim: MS revealed enrichment of disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain-containing protein 10 (ADAM10), which mediates CD40L release as a soluble trimer from T cells upon CD40 engagement.
source: MS also revealed enrichment of disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain-containing protein 10 (ADAM10), which mediates CD40L release as a soluble trimer from T cells upon CD40 engagement (Yacoub et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by mass spectrometry data and cited literature.

claim: GI254023X which displays a higher selectivity for ADAM10 but not TAPI-2 resulted in more CD40L transfer to BSLB.
source: GI254023X which displays a higher selectivity for ADAM10 but not TAPI-2 resulted in more CD40L transfer to BSLB.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5 supplement 3.

claim: A similar increase in CD40L transfer to BSLB was observed following suppression with CRISPR/CAS9-ADAM10 gRNA RNP complex.
source: A similar increase in CD40L transfer to BSLB was observed following suppression with CRISPR/CAS9-ADAM10 gRNA RNP complex.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by CRISPR gene editing and flow cytometry data in Figure 5 supplement 3.

claim: Metalloprotease dependent cleavage of CD40L is not required for synaptic transfer of vesicular CD40L to BSLB.
source: This result suggests that metalloprotease dependent cleavage of CD40L is not required for synaptic transfer of vesicular CD40L to BSLB.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is an inference from the data.

claim: The average diameter of SE was 84 ± 5 nm.
source: In agreement with earlier electron microscopy measurements (Choudhuri et al., 2014), the average diameter of SE was 84 ± 5 nm (Figure 6B–D) and 36 ± 3 SE were transferred per IS (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by dSTORM imaging data in Figure 6B-D.

claim: 36 ± 3 SE were transferred per IS.
source: In agreement with earlier electron microscopy measurements (Choudhuri et al., 2014), the average diameter of SE was 84 ± 5 nm (Figure 6B–D) and 36 ± 3 SE were transferred per IS (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by dSTORM imaging data in Figure 6E.

claim: The number and size of TCR microclusters transferred on SEs is similar to that of TCR microclusters present in the early IS.
source: The number and size of TCR microclusters transferred on SEs is similar to that of TCR microclusters present in the early IS (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by dSTORM imaging data in Figure 6F-H.

claim: TCR microclusters are converted into SE.
source: This provides further evidence that TCR microclusters are converted into SE.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is an inference from the data.

claim: Three color dSTORM revealed 3 subsets of SE: 1) TCR only, 2) CD40L, ICOS or BST2 only and 3) double positive for TCR and CD40L (54.5%), ICOS (77.5%) or BST2 (75.0%).
source: Three color dSTORM revealed 3 subsets of SE: 1) TCR only, 2) CD40L, ICOS or BST2 only and 3) double positive for TCR and CD40L (54.5%), ICOS (77.5%) or BST2 (75.0%) (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by dSTORM imaging data in Figure 7B and supplements.

claim: TCR clusters were colocalized with ICOS or BST2 within a search radius of 50 nm, and segregated from CD40L clusters.
source: TCR clusters were colocalized with ICOS or BST2 within a search radius of 50 nm, and segregated from CD40L clusters (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by CBC analysis in Figure 7C.

claim: There was a high correlation between TCR with ICOS or BST2 at inter-particle distances less than 50 nm, whereas TCR and CD40L showed the highest correlation at a distance of 150 nm.
source: There was a high correlation between TCR with ICOS or BST2 at inter-particle distances less than 50 nm, whereas TCR and CD40L showed the highest correlation at a distance of 150 nm (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by cross-correlation analysis in Figure 7D and supplement 3.

claim: The mean nearest-neighbor distance (NND) of paired single-molecule localizations was 34 nm for TCR and BST2, 17 nm for TCR and ICOS and 230 nm for TCR and CD40L.
source: Corroborating this, the mean nearest-neighbor distance (NND) of paired single-molecule localizations was 34 nm for TCR and BST2, 17 nm for TCR and ICOS and 230 nm for TCR and CD40L (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by NND analysis in Figure 7E.

claim: TCR, BST2 and ICOS occupy overlapping microclusters, whereas TCR and CD40L occupied spatially distinct microclusters that are sorted within single SE.
source: The results are consistent with TCR, BST2 and ICOS occupying overlapping microclusters, whereas TCR and CD40L occupied spatially distinct microclusters that are sorted within single SE.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is an inference from the dSTORM data.

claim: CD40L high SE triggered high expression levels of HLA-DR and CD83.
source: CD40L high SE triggered high expression levels of HLA-DR and CD83 (Figure 8A,B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 8A,B.

claim: CD40L high SE significantly increased release of 46 factors, prominently including several chemokines and inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and IL-12p70.
source: Analysis of 105 secreted factors from DC, revealed that CD40L high SE significantly increased release of 46 factors, prominently including several chemokines and inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and IL-12p70, which are important pro-inflammatory cytokines from licensed DCs (Cella et al., 1996) (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by cytokine array data in Figure 8C.

claim: SE have an active form of CD40L that is sufficient to induce DC maturation in the absence of T cells.
source: These results demonstrate that SE have an active form of CD40L that is sufficient to induce DC maturation in the absence of T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is an inference from the DC activation data.

claim: The density of CD40L on SE is estimated to be over 200 trimers/µm2.
source: Given this small surface area, the density of CD40L on SE is estimated to be over 200 trimers/µm2 (Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is a calculation based on the data.

claim: Vesicular CD40L is a superior agonist compared to soluble CD40L.
source: We observed a significant upregulation of HLA-DR, CD40, ICAM-1, CD80 and CD86 on moDC treated with vesicular CD40L compared to an equivalent concentration of soluble CD40L trimers (Figure 8E–F) demonstrating that vesicular CD40L is a superior agonist compared to soluble CD40L.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 8E-F.

claim: BSLB offer a scalable platform to analyze SE by flow cytometry and mass spectroscopy.
source: Importantly, we adopted BSLB as a scalable platform to analyze SE by flow cytometry and mass spectroscopy.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a methodological contribution.

claim: Each BSLB carries the output from one T cell, on average.
source: The strength of this approach is that each BSLB carries the output from one T cell, on average, such that the output of single IS can be quantified and calibrated to number of antibody binding sites and compared to average levels of the same molecules on the donor T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a methodological consideration.

claim: There is a high degree of enrichment for ligated cargo like ICOS and CD40L (>10%), tetraspannins and BST2 (~10%), and proteins with known tetraspannin association, like MHC class I (1–10%).
source: However, there is a high degree of enrichment for ligated cargo like ICOS and CD40L (>10%), tetraspannins (Théry et al., 2001) and BST2 (34) (~10%), and proteins with known tetraspannin association, like MHC class I (1–10%).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by the data.

claim: Most other proteins are transferred at a level similar to the area of membrane transferred (~0.2%).
source: In contrast, most other proteins are transferred at a level similar to the area of membrane transferred (~0.2%).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by the data.

source: Furthermore, CRISPR gene editing of TSG101 and VPS4 clearly reduced the transfer of TCR and CD40L, further demonstrating specificity for ESCRT dependent vesicle formation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by the data.

claim: BST2 may tether some SE to the T cell membrane, accounting for dragging of SE behind kinapses.
source: BST2 may tether some SE to the T cell membrane, accounting for dragging of SE behind kinapses, and may provide a mechanism for NF-κB signaling in the T cell in response to SE formation (Edgar et al., 2016; Neil et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is a speculation based on the data and cited literature.

claim: BST2 may provide a mechanism for NF-κB signaling in the T cell in response to SE formation.
source: BST2 may tether some SE to the T cell membrane, accounting for dragging of SE behind kinapses, and may provide a mechanism for NF-κB signaling in the T cell in response to SE formation (Edgar et al., 2016; Neil et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is a speculation based on the data and cited literature.

source: TCR engagement independent IS-like structures may allow T cells to more closely inspect APC for presence of relevant pMHC.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is a speculation.

claim: Conditional knockout of CD40L in CD4+ T cells appears to fully account for the classical defects in antibody class switching and T cell help associated with CD40L deficiency.
source: However, conditional knockout of CD40L in CD4+ T cells appears to fully account for the classical defects in antibody class switching and T cell help associated with CD40L deficiency (Horrillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: Platelet CD40L appears to function as an integrin ligand in blood clotting such that its physiological function is not CD40 dependent, but integrin β3 dependent.
source: Instead, platelet CD40L appears to function as an integrin ligand in blood clotting such that its physiological function is not CD40 dependent, but integrin β3 dependent (André et al., 2002).

claim: T cell SEs are generated in an antigen dependent manner and TCR and CD40L are often present in the same SE, thus adding another level of specificity of this post-T cell product.

claim: SE may provide an explanation for reports of antigen specific helper factors.
source: SE may provide an explanation for reports of antigen specific helper factors (Guy et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is a speculation based on the data and cited literature.

claim: SE with TCR and CD40L could account for antigen-specific and MHC-restricted factors that delivered T cell help.
source: Whilst Guy et al suggested a proteolytically cleaved form of TCR that is complexed with other proteins, our study suggests the alternative that SE with TCR and CD40L could account for such an activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is a speculation based on the data.

claim: T cells transfer CD40L to B cells in an agonist pMHC and CD40 dependent manner.
source: T cells transfer CD40L to B cells in an agonist pMHC and CD40 dependent manner (Gardell and Parker, 2017).

claim: Active processes in the B cells are required to use CD40 to capture CD40L from a T cell without a TCR agonist to form an IS.
source: This suggests that active processes in the B cells are required to use CD40 to capture CD40L from a T cell without a TCR agonist to form an IS.

claim: DC also receive CD40L-CD40 signals without cognate pMHC.
source: A recent study suggests that DC also receive CD40L-CD40 signals without cognate pMHC (Pasqual et al., 2018).

claim: The physical segregation of CD40L from the attachment site to the antigen-presenting surface may in part explain its availability to both the anti-CD40L antibody used for detection and CD40 on DCs.
source: This physical segregation of CD40L from the attachment site to the antigen-presenting surface may in part explain its availability to both the anti-CD40L antibody used for detection and CD40 on DCs, which responded functionally to the CD40L on SE.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is an inference from the data.
